Australian Grains Industry Community Trust Collaboration Blueprint.

Description: Trust among rural and urban communities is vital to ensure Australian grain growers are able to conduct business with minimal disruption and continue to innovate and adopt new technologies. In many cases, trust is something that only becomes apparent when it is broken or tested. Measures of trust in the grains industry by the Australian community have changed over time, with a small decrease since 2020. Decreasing trust can lead to increased regulation, limited market access, disincentives to invest in infrastructure, and reduced industry productivity, profitability and sustainability. Poor levels of trust within an industry make it more likely to be under high levels of scrutiny for practices used on farm, more likely to struggle with talent attraction for future workforce requirements (both on farm and in support and research roles) and reduce the ability for innovation, such as automation, to be adopted as commonplace on farm. There is a high risk that not addressing or maintaining current levels of trust within the grains sector will lead to future challenges impacting grain producers ability to maintain profitability and adopt new technology. GRDC is seeking a service provider to conduct stakeholder analysis, mapping and consultation to establish clear roles and responsibilities for developing community trust activities in the grains sector. It will bring grains industry stakeholders together, including peak bodies, to develop clear definitions and guidelines for working through issues relating to community trust. The developed blueprint will consequently help guide future activities, including use cases of a data and insights program, a pilot industry communication development program and future education-based activities. Critically, the blueprint requires multi-stakeholder ownership for it to succeed. Getting this right will enable clear GRDC roles and functions that can be used to inform areas of potential investment that can support collaborative industry efforts to build community trust and address industry challenges. This investment will contribute towards building positive, proactive relationships with the broader community to allow continued innovation, reduce potential innovation bottlenecks and support grain growers with freedom to operate. Outcome: By December 2027, deliver a community trust collaboration blueprint for the Australian Grains Industry. Outputs. Output 1. Title: Development of a Community Trust Collaboration Blueprint for the Australia Grains Industry. Description: By December 2027, deliver a community trust collaboration blueprint for the Australian Grains Industry. This will be used to inform GRDC involvement in community trust activities and guide future proposed programs of work. The blueprint will include: · Establishing the definition of community trust across the sector, and its role in building industry sustainability and specify outcomes. · Mapping stakeholders, undertaking stakeholder identification and prioritisation and define roles, responsibilities, and best practices for trust building, including open and effective engagement, co-planning strategies and community investment programs. · Outcomes from a stakeholder workshop to discuss areas for potential collaboration · Using existing resources, define the quantitative trust baseline, and model and use existing trust drivers to inform objectives for key areas of collaboration. · Review existing information and consultancies relating to community trust to inform how proposed investment is structured. In consultation with GRDC a position statement outlining GRDC’s responsibilities and scope aligned to the blueprint will be drafted for GRDC use.

Notice of RFT - Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel of Outreach Program Counsellors for the

This is a pre-release notice to provide advance notification of a proposed RFT for the Refresh and Expansion of the Professions of the Panel. Please note, eligibility, application requirements, assessment processes, and contractual arrangements will be set out in the forthcoming RFT. No evaluation criteria, scoring methodology, or commercial terms are being released at this stage. The Department reserves the right to modify or cancel the proposed RFT at its discretion. Background on Open Arms Open Arms is Australia’s national accredited provider of mental health and wellbeing services for veterans and the families of veterans. Open Arms provides mental health counselling, relationship counselling, peer support services, and group programs for people with Australian Defence Force (ADF) service (current and former serving members) and their immediate families. Open Arms provides free and confidential counselling through a national network of multidisciplinary mental health professionals, delivered in dedicated Open Arms centres by the DVA’s staff, or through the Panel; being a network of accredited mental health clinicians, engaged to support the delivery of services on behalf of Open Arms across Australia through the Outreach Program. Open Arms can provide counselling, care coordination and peer support services to veterans and the families of veterans within an episode of care model, where clients engage with our services for goal directed interventions for a defined period. Open Arms aims to provide timely access to appropriate services and care, based on a comprehensive holistic assessment and integrated care pathways to meet client needs and support recovery. This includes working in partnership with health systems, including primary health, as well as other community agencies to ensure comprehensive support for our clients. Background on the Panel and Outreach Program Open Arms’ Model of Care provides the organisational framework that underpins the delivery of all Outreach Program services. It guides how we support veterans and the families of veterans through trauma-informed, military-aware, recovery-oriented care, while ensuring consistent clinical governance, quality service delivery and positive client outcomes. In 2024 the Panel was established through which Outreach Providers provide Open Arms services to clients. The Panel is the mechanism for Open Arms to engage with Outreach Providers to ensure the highest level of support can be delivered to clients. Only organisations or individuals appointed to the Panel can provide Open Arms Outreach Program Counselling Services. The categories of services that are delivered through the Panel include: Outreach Program Counsellors (OPCs), who provide individual, couples, or family counselling Group Program Facilitators (GPFs), who facilitate evidence-informed, military-aware group programs that strengthen resilience, build practical skills, and promote wellbeing Clinical Supervisors, who provide professional supervision to Open Arms’ staff. Outreach Providers on the Panel can provide one, two or all three service streams, depending on their qualifications, experience and the services they are approved to deliver. Go to the Open Arms website for further information: https://www.openarms.gov.au/about/open-arms-outreach-program Expansion of definition of OPC In 2025 the Veterans’ Entitlements (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025 and the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation (Treatment Principles) Amendment (Outreach Program Counsellor) Determination 2025), were enacted which amended the MRCA Treatment Principles (No. MRCC 53/2013) and the Treatment Principles (Instrument 2013 No. R52) – (collectively the Treatment Principles) – to expand the types of professions who can provide Outreach Program Counselling as an Outreach Program Counsellor (OPC). Now that occupational therapists, registered nurses, social workers (general) and counsellors are recognised as additional profession types eligible to apply to become a provider, the Department wishes to update the Panel accordingly through the proposed RFT. The Department is therefore looking to procure Outreach Providers from the following eligible professions: a person who is registered with AHPRA as a psychologist; a person who is registered with AHPRA as an occupational therapist; a person who is registered with AHPRA as a registered nurse; a person who is eligible for membership with the Australian Association of Social Workers; or a person who is registered: as a registered clinical counsellor with the Psychotherapy and Counselling Federation of Australia; as a counsellor at registration category Level 3 or Level 4 with the Australian Counselling Association Limited. The Department is currently planning to release the RFT to market through publication on AusTender in September 2026, however this timeframe may be subject to change. Please note that this is not an RFT and does not commit the Department to proceed. The Close Date and Time stated in this notice relates to this pre-release notice only and does not reflect the proposed RFT commencement and closing dates for potential tenderers to lodge their submissions. The RFT, where undertaken, will be published on AusTender and will include the Closing Date and Time for lodgement of submissions.

Southern Region pulse research, demonstration, and extension

GRDC is investing in a new Southern Region investment to improve the profitability and adoption of pulse crops within farming systems. Pulses are already an important component of these systems, with recent growth driven by lentil production in Victoria and South Australia and expansion into new environments. However, as pulse intensity increases, constraints such as soil acidity and subsoil limitations, herbicide resistance and residue risks, greater disease pressure under tighter pulse sequences, and seasonal variability are becoming more prominent. These challenges, along with emerging opportunities, are identified in GRDC’s pulse crop improvement plans. To address them, the investment will use a regional “hub and spoke” model that combines rigorous field research with practical, paddock-scale learning. Hub sites will target key knowledge gaps, while spoke sites will deliver locally relevant trials, demonstrations, field days and workshops that support growers and advisers and generate high-quality industry datasets. The Regional Pulse Advisory Committee and relevant grower and adviser networks will help set annual priorities for each agroecological zone, supported by expertise from the National Pulse Coordination and Strategy Program in agronomy, crop protection, rhizobia, soils, trial design, data analysis, extension and markets. This approach will retain the flexibility to respond as regional priorities and opportunities evolve.

Western Region pulse research, demonstration, and extension

GRDC is proposing a new Western Region investment to help more growers profitably include pulse crops in their farming systems. Pulses such as lupins, lentils, chickpeas and faba beans improve rotations, add nitrogen and support more diverse, profitable systems, yet adoption in Western Australia remains limited by practical barriers around establishment, weed and disease management, harvestability, market access, storage and confidence in local performance. The investment proposes a regional "hub and spoke" model that links practical paddock-scale learning with rigorous field research, with hub sites addressing key knowledge gaps and spoke sites delivering locally relevant trials, demonstrations, field days and workshops that benefit growers and advisers while generating quality datasets for industry. Local grower groups, advisers and stakeholders will shape annual priorities for each agro-ecological zone, drawing on the National Pulse Coordination and Strategy program for expertise in agronomy, crop protection, rhizobia, soils, trial design, data analysis, extension and markets, with flexibility to adjust as opportunities change. By 2032, the investment aims to equip Western Region growers and advisers with the knowledge and confidence to increase pulse production and improve gross margins, strengthening pulse agronomy capability in Western Australia and leaving a better-connected legacy of trial results, resources and practical guidance.
The National Pulse Expansion, Improvement, and Adoption Program - National Coordination and Strategy Function

This procurement seeks a suitably qualified applicant to establish and deliver the National Coordination and Strategy Function for the National Pulse Expansion, Improvement and Adoption Program. The successful provider will work with the Regional Pulse RD&E to baseline adoption, understand barriers and drivers of adoption and set strategic evidence-based adoption targets for key pulses in each agroecological zone. The provider will coordinate national meetings and support Regional pulse RD&E projects with reporting processes and plans as well as drive the two-way sharing of information and key learnings between the Regional pulse RD&E projects and other key GRDC investments in pulses. This coordination role will ensure that regional activities contribute to the nationally coordinated outcome of improving the profitability and adoption of pulse crops across Australian grain-growing regions.

Enhancing wheat adaptability for stable yields under variable climates: an integrated genetic and agronomic approach

Climate variability is making Australian wheat production more challenging, with drought and interacting stresses such as heat, nutrient limitation and soil constraints increasingly affecting crop performance across regions and seasons. These stresses can reduce yield stability and create greater seasonal risk for growers. One opportunity to address this challenge is to better understand and use wheat’s adaptive plasticity-the ability of wheat plants to adjust growth, development and resource use in response to changing conditions. Adaptive plasticity may help crops reduce yield loss in dry or stressful seasons while maintaining yield potential when conditions are favourable. While wheat breeding programs select for broad adaptation, the specific traits, benchmarks and selection approaches that support adaptive plasticity are not yet routinely defined or targeted. Through this investment, GRDC aims to identify, validate and translate priority plasticity traits into breeder-ready knowledge, datasets, genetic resources and selection guidance. This EOI seeks to identify capable Respondents to participate in a potential multi-stage procurement process to deliver this work.

Developing acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties to expand faba bean adaption.

Faba bean production in Australia is constrained by soil acidity, particularly in Western Australia, South Australia, southern New South Wales and parts of Victoria, where acidic soils reduce root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop vigour and grain yield. Soil acidity also limits the expansion of faba bean into otherwise suitable production environments. While liming remains an important soil management practice, sub-surface acidity is often difficult, slow and costly to remediate, creating a need for complementary genetic solutions that improve crop performance and profitability on affected soils. Recent GRDC investments have successfully delivered acid-tolerant rhizobia for faba bean, improving nodulation and nitrogen fixation under low pH conditions. However, the effectiveness of these inoculants depends on successful plant-rhizobia interactions, and current elite faba bean germplasm remains poorly adapted to acid soils (pH (CaCl2) <5.0). Developing acid-soil-tolerant varieties is therefore essential to fully realise the benefits of improved rhizobia strains and maximise productivity in acidic soil environments. This four-year investment will accelerate the development of acid-soil-tolerant faba bean varieties by delivering the germplasm, genetic knowledge and breeding tools required to support long-term genetic improvement. The investment will identify and validate novel sources of acid soil tolerance from Australian and international germplasm, improve understanding of the physiological, biochemical and genetic mechanisms underpinning tolerance, and translate these discoveries into practical breeding outcomes for Australian faba bean breeding programs. Controlled-environment screening, field-based validation and modern genomic approaches will identify and characterise traits associated with improved performance on acidic soils, including traits linked to root growth, nodulation, nitrogen fixation, crop establishment and yield. Activities should address both surface and sub-surface soil acidity and generate robust, field-relevant data to support breeding and selection decisions across target production environments. A key component of the investment will be the development of validated high-throughput phenotyping methods, screening protocols and molecular markers that enable efficient selection for acid soil tolerance. These tools will support more rapid and cost-effective identification and deployment of favourable alleles within breeding pipelines, accelerating genetic gain for adaptation to acidic soils. Breeder-ready germplasm will incorporate novel acid-soil-tolerance alleles and demonstrating improved performance under acidic soil conditions, with a target yield advantage of at least 10% over benchmark varieties grown on acid soils of pH (CaCl2) below 5.0. Germplasm should be validated across representative production environments and supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and marker datasets to facilitate immediate use in breeding programs. Strong collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to guide trait prioritisation, validation environments, phenotyping approaches and deployment pathways, ensuring outputs align with breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs. The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the genetic resources, screening tools and knowledge required to develop future faba bean varieties with improved adaptation to acid soils, enhanced yield stability and increased productivity. These advances will complement existing soil amelioration practices and acid-tolerant rhizobia, support expansion into suitable regions, improve reliability on acid soils and strengthen the competitiveness and sustainability of the Australian faba bean industry.
Enhancing faba bean seed colour and seed size uniformity to increase the value of faba beans and reduce risk of classifi

Faba bean is an important Australian pulse crop and export commodity, supplying premium food and feed markets where visual grain quality is a key determinant of market access, classification and value. Buyers place strong emphasis on seed coat colour, colour retention and seed size uniformity, with these traits directly influencing grading outcomes, market acceptance and the price received throughout the value chain. Variability in visual grain quality, together with seed coat darkening during storage and handling, can increase the risk of downgrades, reduce grower returns and weaken Australia’s competitive advantage in premium export markets. Although visual grain quality is known to have a strong genetic component, the biological, biochemical and environmental factors influencing seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity are not well understood. Australian breeding programs currently have limited access to the genetic resources, molecular markers and high-throughput phenotyping tools needed to efficiently improve these traits. Recent advances in genomics, artificial intelligence, digital imaging and data analytics provide new opportunities to accelerate genetic gain and develop more effective breeding solutions. This four-year investment will develop the knowledge, genetic resources and breeding-enabling tools required to improve seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity in Australian faba beans. The investment will investigate the genetic, physiological, biochemical and environmental drivers underlying visual grain quality, including the mechanisms responsible for seed coat oxidation and post-harvest darkening. Activities should consider both genetic and non-genetic contributors to trait expression, including the effects of storage conditions, handling practices and environmental influences on grain quality outcomes. A key component of the investment will be the development and validation of modern phenotyping and analytical tools to enable routine selection for visual grain quality traits. This includes the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital imaging and high-throughput phenotyping approaches to objectively measure seed coat colour stability, seed size uniformity and other commercially important visual attributes. Identification and incorporation of valuable genetic variation for improved seed coat colour stability and seed size uniformity will enable development of breeder-ready germplasm for use in Australian faba bean breeding programs. Germplasm should demonstrate measurable improvements in visual grain quality traits and be supported by associated genetic, phenotypic and validated molecular marker datasets to facilitate rapid integration into breeding pipelines. Strong and ongoing collaboration with Australian commercial and public faba bean breeding programs will be a core requirement of the investment. Breeding programs should be engaged throughout the project to help guide trait prioritisation, phenotyping methods, validation activities and deployment pathways. This will ensure outputs are aligned with market requirements and breeding priorities and can be rapidly incorporated into crossing blocks, breeding pipelines and early-generation selection programs. The intended outcome is to provide Australian breeders with the germplasm, molecular markers, phenotyping tools and knowledge required to accelerate the development of future faba bean varieties with improved visual grain quality, greater market suitability and reduced risk of classification downgrades. These advances will help maintain existing market premiums, improve storage and marketing flexibility, protect Australia's reputation as a supplier of high-quality faba beans and strengthen the long-term competitiveness and value of the Australian faba bean industry.

Program 3B - Improved use of bait products for pest snail management

This investment will deliver applied RD&E to improve the reliability and effectiveness of existing pest snail bait products under realistic field conditions. The successful provider will generate practical guidance on bait rate, pellet density, timing and performance under different seasonal, pest snail species and farming-system conditions. The work is intended to help growers and advisers better understand when baiting is likely to be effective, why performance may vary, and how bait-use decisions can be improved as part of integrated pest snail management. Findings will be developed in forms suitable for extension and decision support through the broader coordinated pest snail investment.
Program 2 - National extension and adviser capability to support adoption of effective pest snail management

This investment will deliver a sustained national extension and adviser capability program to support adoption of effective pest snail management. The successful provider will work with growers, advisers, regional networks and pest snail technical experts to translate existing and emerging knowledge into practical, regionally relevant guidance and decision support. The program will focus on strengthening adviser capability, supporting peer-to-peer learning and demonstration, and improving grower confidence and decision-making across key snail-affected regions.
Program 1 - National coordination, integration, synthesis and learning for pest snail management

This investment will establish the coordination and integration function for GRDC’s broader pest snail management investment. The successful provider will establish and operate a Program Advisory Committee, support whole-of-program planning and review, coordinate synthesis and learning across the related pest snail programs, and help ensure emerging findings, risks and priorities are shared in a timely and consistent way. The role is intended to improve alignment across the investment, avoid duplication, and support practical management outcomes for Australian grain growers and advisers.
Program 3A - Pest snail ecology, population dynamics and risk prediction

This investment will deliver applied RD&E to improve understanding of pest snail ecology, population dynamics and risk prediction in Australian grain systems. The successful provider will build on existing GRDC investments, datasets and tools to develop practical, regionally relevant decision rules for snail activity, bait timing, harvest contamination risk and feasible harvest-phase mitigation options. Findings will be developed in forms suitable for extension and decision support through the broader coordinated pest snail investment.

The Commonwealth as represented by the Australian Institute of Criminology (AIC) is seeking sumissions for the Criminology Research Fund 2026. The Criminology Research Fund (CRF) program is a competitive program that provides funds to support the conduct of high quality, policy-relevant research projects in the area of crime and criminal justice. The CRF is funded through annual contributions by the Commonwealth, State and Territory Governments. The CRF program is administered by the AIC on the basis of recommendations from the Criminology Research Advisory Council (Advisory Council). The Advisory Council, which includes representatives from each of the contributing Governments, provides recommendations to the Director of the AIC on research priorities and an assessment of applications made under the annual CRF program. The Advisory Council bases its assessment on the recommendations of an Academic Panel chaired by the Academic Advisor (an AIC research staff member). The AIC will award contracts in varying values.
